# Liming and marling of sour soils (`liming_marling`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Deps: helped by lime_burning, acids_bases_ph
- Core idea: Rain-washed, sandy and heath soils turn sour (acid): sorrel, heather and moss thrive, clover and barley fail. Spreading ground chalk, limestone, marl (limy clay) or slaked lime, a few tonnes per hectare every several years, neutralises the acid, lets clover and beans grow and makes dung work better. Test the material: real marl or chalk fizzes in strong vinegar.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating lime as a fertiliser; it unlocks nutrients but supplies almost none, hence 'lime and lime without manure makes both farm and farmer poor'
  - Liming soil that is already chalky, which locks up iron and manganese and harms the crop
  - Mixing quicklime or fresh slaked lime with dung, which drives the nitrogen off as ammonia
  - Handling quicklime carelessly; it burns skin and eyes and heats violently with water
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny describes marling by the Gauls and Britons, with different marls for different soils (Natural History XVII); Varro saw it on the Rhine; europe: 13th c. – marl pits common in England and northern France; 18th c. liming general with cheap coal-burnt lime; 1909 Sørensen defines pH; china: by Song – lime applied to acid paddy soils in the south
- Read:
  - Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia XVII.42–48
  - E. John Russell, Soil Conditions and Plant Growth (1912)
